analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction drug makers get for advertising prescription drugs directly to consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from July 2002 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Prescription drug companies can deduct the cost of their TV and magazine ads aimed at consumers as a business expense, meaning taxpayers effectively help pay for those ads. This bill would remove that deduction, so drug makers would pay the full cost of the advertising themselves. It was introduced in July 2002 and never moved out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers. Removing the deduction would make drug ads more expensive for manufacturers, likely shrinking an ad campaign that encourages demand for expensive brand-name drugs, and it would end a tax subsidy that other taxpayers otherwise cover.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to the tax code disallowing any deduction for expenses of a direct-to-consumer advertisement for a prescription drug, effective for amounts paid after December 31, 2002 [S3] [S2].

Today those ad costs are treated like any other business expense, so a portion of the cost is effectively borne by all taxpayers; the bill shifts that cost back onto the drug companies that choose to advertise [S2].

Direct-to-consumer ads push patients toward heavily promoted brand-name drugs; making manufacturers bear the full cost of that advertising could reduce pressure on consumers to choose higher-priced drugs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers would pay more in taxes by losing the deduction, and television networks, magazines, and advertising businesses would lose revenue from the multibillion-dollar stream of drug ads.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and TV/media ad revenue

drawbacks.text: The tax code currently allows businesses generally to deduct advertising costs; singling out prescription drug ads for disallowance treats one form of commercial speech differently, which critics view as using tax policy to discourage protected speech.
Broadcasters and magazines depend on pharmaceutical advertising as a major revenue source, so the bill would cut income for media companies and could reduce advertising-supported programming [S2].

The bill does not ban the ads or lower drug prices directly; its effect depends on drug makers responding to the higher after-tax cost by advertising less, and it would raise no revenue from companies that do not advertise to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is indirect but real: drug advertising costs would no longer be partially subsidized by taxpayers, and the incentive to promote expensive brand-name drugs directly to patients would shrink. The costs fall on a specific industry and the media companies that carry its ads, which is exactly what the bill is designed to do. The main design weakness is that it works through incentives rather than directly affecting drug prices, so the consumer benefit depends on how manufacturers respond. On balance a modest, targeted measure whose costs land on a concentrated industry and whose benefits are diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on July 11, 2002, with Representative Joseph Crowley as the other original sponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
Five members cosponsored the bill — four House Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent — and no further action was ever recorded [S4] [S5].
The Ways and Means Committee, which holds jurisdiction over the tax code, held no hearing or markup, and the bill received no floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers keep a tax deduction for consumer-directed advertising, and the broadcasters and magazines that sell that advertising keep the revenue. No consumer action was required to preserve the status quo; the bill simply never moved.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican supported it, and the Republican-chaired tax committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill would end the tax deduction drug companies claim for consumer-directed ads, raising their after-tax cost of marketing brand-name drugs directly to patients. Drug makers' interest in keeping the deduction runs against consumers, who face ad-driven demand for higher-priced drugs and effectively help subsidize the ads through the tax code.
Pharmaceutical advertising is a major revenue source for television networks and print media. If drug makers paid the full cost of ads, the industry expected less advertising to be purchased.
